AM is gaining popularity for part manufacturing that can directly compete with traditional manufacturing methods such as subtractive, joining, or formative (Conner et al., 2014).
For example, binder jetting offers a versatile range of materials for fabrication, and is currently being utilized for sand mold and casting applications (Wohlers, 2017).
Inconel alloys are known as superalloys because of their excellent mechanical strength and resistance to creep and corrosion in harsh environments.
The mechanical properties evaluated include ultimate tensile strength (UTS), yield strength (YS), percent elongation and modulus of elasticity.
The first powder-bed-based AM technology explored in this comparison was binder jetting.
It is an AM process in which parts are fabricated in a layer-by-layer fashion using a polymer-based or aqueous binder.
A roller mechanism is utilized to spread the precursor powder onto a powder bed.
The powder particles are subsequently joined together through the deposition of binder, using a piezo-driven print head, according to a CAD design.
The deposited binder is treated by an infrared heating system, slightly hardening the layer to allow the spreading of a new powder layer to take place.
This process is repeated until the part is complete.
The curing cycle, performed on the entire powder bed, further hardens the printed part (green body), creating a brown body capable of withstanding the subsequent removal of unwanted powder.
This process takes place in an oven at temperatures of 195 C ours (1 hour for \~ 1 h per 10 mm of part height.

The final step in the creation of a dense part, sintering, is performed on the brown body at elevated temperatures necessary to initiate sintering, usually ranging from 0.5 to 0.8 times the melting point $( \mathrm { T } _ { \mathrm { m } , }$ 12901350 °C for Inconel 625), allowing the powder particles to fuse together (Anon., 2018).

One advantage of binder jetting over other powder-bed-based technologies is its ability to manufacture parts using a wider range of materials, including ceramics, metals, polymers and sand (Gaytan et al., 2015).
As per ISO/ASTM 52900, powder bed fusion is defined as "an additive manufacturing process in which thermal energy selectively fuses regions of a powder bed" (ASTM International, 2015).
The fabrication of metal components is achieved by controlling the powder fusion to a prescribed region at the given layer as commanded by a CAD design, followed by the creation of a new layer.
As previously mentioned, the two most common forms of powder bed fusion are EPBF and LPBF, which are described in further detail in the following sub-sections as well as characterized and compared.
The EPBF process is an AM technique used for fabrication of metallic components through the use of an electron beam as the energy source to melt powder particles together.
The process can be broken down into three major steps: (1) raking of a powder layer, (2) preheating of powder particles (sintering), and (3) melting of the powder particles.
After a particular layer is melted, the build platform is lowered one layer height (5070 µm) and the process is repeated until the fabrication is complete.
The LPBF process accomplishes the fusion of powder particles with the use of a laser beam as the thermal energy source.
Commercially available parameters for LPBF enable for fabrication of parts at layer heights that usually range from 20 to 70 µm.

However, its performance relies highly on absorbed water molecules, and dehydration under low humidity drastically lowers its proton conductivity [7], thereby limiting its suitability as a solid electrolyte for proton batteries.
In recent years, COFs have attracted growing interest in the field of proton conduction [10-14].

Moreover, most current efforts have focused on COF-based protonic electrolytes for $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } / \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ fuel cell applications [2325], where the high proton conductivity of the electrolytes was mainly observed under high humidity or at elevated temperature.

As a result, the electrolyte exhibited outstanding proton conductivity $( > 1 0 ^ { - 2 } \thinspace \mathrm { S } \thinspace \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 } )$ under ambient conditions, and excellent long-term stability, surpassing all COF-based electrolytes reported thus far.

As depicted in Figure 1a, both the zwitterionic vinylene-linked COF (ZVCOF) and its non-zwitterionic counterpart (NVCOF) were synthesized through a Knoevenagel condensation reaction between 1,3,5- tri(4-formylphenyl)triazine (TFPT) and either N-sulfopropyl-2,4,6-trimethylpyridinium (SPTMP) or 2,4,6-trimethylpyridine (TMP) [32, 33], respectively.
Powder x-ray diffraction (PXRD) patterns revealed that both COFs exhibit high crystallinity (Figure 1b,c).
The pore diameters were estimated to be 1.3 nm for ZVCOF and 1.7 nm for NVCOF, in good agreement with the predicted values from the simulated structures.
This observed difference between the two COFs is attributed to their different affinities for PA, as supported by contact angle measurements shown in Figure 2b.
PA@NVCOF-X (X = 40- 60) also showed similar surface area and pore volume values, suggesting negligible residual porosity upon PA loading.
To this date, the high proton conductivity of most previously reported COF-based proton conductors could only be achieved under high humidity or at elevated temperatures above 100°C (Table S1).

These findings suggest the formation of robust hydrogen-bonding networks between PA molecules and the sulfonate groups in ZVCOF, which facilitates a continuous and efficient proton-transfer pathway, accounting for the superior proton conduction of ZvCOF-based electrolytes.

Encouraged by their excellent electrochemical performance, the practical applicability of the solid-state proton batteries was showcased using six batteries connected in series to power a 3-watt LED bulb (Figure 4b).
The successful light-up of the LED bulb highlights our proton batteries' potential for real-world energy storage applications.
In addition to a higher capacity, our proton batteries' electrochemical stability and cyclability were also found to be superior to those of batteries assembled with liquid acid electrolytes.
Firstly, due to the absence of free water molecules, solid protonic electrolytes typically exhibit a broader electrochemical stability window compared to conventional liquid acid counterparts.

After 5000 charge-discharge cycles, the XRD pattern of the $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ membrane electrode in the solid-state proton battery exhibited distinct diffraction peaks similar to those of the freshly prepared $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ (Figure 5b).

While the $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ membrane in the solid-state battery retained its original morphology with minimal structural damage (Figure 5e), severe erosion was observed for the $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ anode in the battery with liquid PA electrolyte (Figure 5f).

This new solid-state proton electrolyte developed in this study can serve as a promising alternative to traditional liquid acid electrolytes, advancing the development of high-performance, long-lasting proton batteries (Figures S36-S38).

The resulting electrolyte exhibited a wide electrochemical stability window of $2 . 7 \mathrm { V } ,$ and the highest proton conductivity of $5 . 3 4 \times 1 0 ^ { - 2 } \mathrm { ~ S ~ c m ^ { - 1 } }$ under ambient conditions among all reported COF-based protonic electrolytes, alongside remarkable long-term stability.

More notably, when integrated into proton batteries, this electrolyte enabled the batteries to achieve outstanding electrochemical performance, including good rate capability, record-high specific capacity of 108.5 mAh $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ at $1 . 0 \mathrm { ~ A ~ g ^ { - 1 } } ,$ , and excellent cycling stability with 90% capacity retention after 2000 charge-discharge cycles at $1 . 0 \mathrm { ~ A ~ g ^ { - 1 } }$ , outperforming the performance of all the previously reported solid-state proton batteries.
This work presents a viable design strategy that leverages zwitterionic functionalities in COFs to develop high-performance solid-state protonic electrolytes for advanced proton battery applications.

While a large number of dislocations are pinned at the whisker-matrix interfaces, the effect is particularly pronounced in regions where multiple whiskers intersect.

The inherent surface roughness of laser-based powder bed fusion (LB-PBF) is detrimental to fatigue strength [16]; with as-manufactured LB-PBF surfaces providing inferior fatigue performance to traditionally manufactured components with machined or processed surfaces [7].
The criticality of surface notches is related to both their depth and sharpness [10].
The surface roughness of LB-PBF components comprises of both primary and secondary roughness [11].

Primary roughness is generated via melt pool solidification and develops notch-like geometries, its formation being dependent on process parameters, including layer thickness and laser-powder interaction [12,13].
This primary roughness creates stress concentrations and facilitates crack initiation under fatigue loading [5,14].
Secondary roughness includes adhered powder particles [15]; and is less critical to fatigue response than primary roughness [14,16,17].

Build orientation is a determining factor to the criticality of surface roughness as downward-facing or overhanging surfaces exhibit higher primary surface roughness than upward-facing surfaces due to gravitational effects on the solidifying melt pool [21] and intimate contact between powder bed and melt pool region [22].
To aid heat transfer and reduce part distortion, downward-facing surfaces may require support structures at acute inclination angles [23], often defined as those being less than 45° [24].

Even if surface processing is applied to these surfaces, there is evidence that insufficient machining depth will not yield significant fatigue life benefits due to deep surface notches being exposed to the surface [6,7].

Nanoparticles or precipitates are long used to block dislocations to strengthen metals.

This is a likely solution to the problem, because an amorphous phase and its interface with the matrix have been reported to act as dislocation sources and sinks7,8, which would help alleviate the stress concentrations at the obstacles.

As such, amorphous nanoparticles would be the dispersion of choice, in delaying damage nucleation to significantly improve ductility and other damagesensitive in-service properties such as fatigue resistance.
The question is then how to realize a dense and uniform dispersion of amorphous nanoparticles inside the metals.

For the reinforcing phase, we set three criteria for the materials selection: (1) high strength and elastic modulus to ensure the desired strengthening; (2) a melting point within a control window (\~ 3000 K) that is accessible to the L-PBF process, such that the dispersions can be turned amorphous via melting, which are then torn apart during turbulent fluid flow and rapidly quenched; and (3) no chemical decomposition or extensive reaction with the matrix pool during the melting of reinforcements"3.
The above criteria led us to a system of simple boron carbide $\mathrm { ( B _ { 4 } C ) }$ reinforced copper as the first model.
